Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Morgan Casey Lee

PURPOSE AND IDENTIFICATION OF THE PROPERTY
This document concerns the following property: Life insurance policy no. 12345 issued by ABC Life, or the residence at 1234 Elm Street, Sacramento, CA 95814 (the "property"), whose character as community property or as the separate property of Jordan Alex Lee or Morgan Casey Lee is in question. The parties married on June 14, 2015. The writing, if any, that is claimed to have changed the property's character is described as: Interspousal transfer grant deed dated March 3, 2021, signed by both spouses. This document states legal background on how California law treats a change in the character of property between spouses during marriage -- a "transmutation" -- and in particular on the requirement, found in Family Code section 852, that such a change be made in writing by an express declaration, as the California Supreme Court has construed that requirement in Estate of MacDonald (1990), In re Marriage of Benson (2005), In re Marriage of Valli (2014), and In re Brace (2020). It is a companion to this project's Postnuptial Agreement and Section 2581 Joint-Title Presumption documents. This document is not a court order, is not a transmutation agreement, and does not state whether the property described above is community property, separate property, or a combination of both.

STATUTE: MARRIED PERSONS MAY TRANSMUTE PROPERTY BY AGREEMENT OR TRANSFER
The Family Code authorizes married persons, by agreement or transfer, with or without consideration, to change the character of their property in three directions: community property to the separate property of either spouse; the separate property of either spouse to community property; and the separate property of one spouse to the separate property of the other. Such a change is called a transmutation. The authorization is expressly subject to the sections that follow it, including the writing and express-declaration requirement of section 852 described in the next clause.

STATUTE: A TRANSMUTATION IS NOT VALID UNLESS MADE IN WRITING BY AN EXPRESS DECLARATION ACCEPTED BY THE ADVERSELY AFFECTED SPOUSE
Section 852, subdivision (a), provides that a transmutation of real or personal property is not valid unless made in writing by an express declaration that is made, joined in, consented to, or accepted by the spouse whose interest in the property is adversely affected. In In re Marriage of Benson (2005), the California Supreme Court read this sentence as imposing three requirements -- the agreement must be in writing, it must contain an express declaration by which the transmutation is made, and it must be accepted in some fashion by the adversely affected spouse -- and observed that the rule is framed in the negative, as though all intendments weigh against finding compliance in the usual case, and that the statute states no exception to the requirement of an express written declaration. Subdivision (b) separately provides that a transmutation of real property is not effective as to third parties without notice of it unless recorded.

CASE LAW: MACDONALD -- WHY THE LEGISLATURE REQUIRED A WRITING (THE PROBLEM OF "EASY TRANSMUTATION")
In Estate of MacDonald (1990), the California Supreme Court construed the express-declaration requirement, then codified at Civil Code section 5110.730, subdivision (a), and now found in Family Code section 852, subdivision (a). The court traced the statute to a 1984 recommendation of the California Law Revision Commission. As the court recounted, the Commission had observed that under prior California law it was quite easy for spouses to transmute both real and personal property, because a transmutation could be found based on oral statements or implications from the conduct of the spouses, and that this rule of easy transmutation had generated extensive litigation in dissolution proceedings and encouraged a spouse, after the marriage ended, to transform a passing comment into an agreement or even to commit perjury by manufacturing an oral or implied transmutation. The court concluded that the statute was intended to remedy problems that arose when courts found transmutations on the basis of evidence the Legislature considered unreliable, and that the Legislature intended not only to invalidate purely oral transmutations but also to invalidate some claimed transmutations even though some form of writing existed.

CASE LAW: MACDONALD -- THE WRITING MUST ITSELF STATE THAT THE CHARACTER OR OWNERSHIP OF THE PROPERTY IS BEING CHANGED
MacDonald held that the statute must be construed to preclude reference to extrinsic evidence in the proof of transmutations. Following its earlier decision in California Trust Co. v. Bennett (1949) construing the joint-tenancy writing requirement, the court concluded that a writing signed by the adversely affected spouse is not an express declaration unless it contains language which expressly states that the characterization or ownership of the property is being changed. The court explained that this reading gives meaning to all the words of the statute, effects the Legislature's intent to create a writing requirement that lets courts validate transmutations without resort to extrinsic evidence, and thereby avoids encouraging perjury and the proliferation of litigation. The court acknowledged that its construction may preclude finding a transmutation in some cases where extrinsic evidence of an intent to transmute exists, and answered that it is precisely such reliance on extrinsic evidence that the Legislature intended to eliminate.

CASE LAW: MACDONALD -- NO PARTICULAR WORDS ARE REQUIRED, BUT A BARE CONSENT FORM WAS NOT ENOUGH
The writings at issue in MacDonald were spousal-consent paragraphs on three standard bank IRA adoption agreements, by which the terminally ill wife consented to her husband's designation of his revocable trust as beneficiary of accounts funded with community pension proceeds. The court held that these writings failed the express-declaration requirement: they contained no language characterizing the pension funds, and it was not possible to tell from the face of the consent paragraphs, or of the adoption agreements as a whole, whether the wife was aware that the legal effect of her signature might be to alter the character or ownership of her interest in the funds. At the same time, the court stated that it did not hold that the statute requires use of the term "transmutation" or any other particular locution; a sufficient writing might contain the words "transmutation," "community property," or "separate property," but need not. By way of example, the court said the consent paragraph would have sufficed had it included an additional sentence reading: "I give to the account holder any interest I have in the funds deposited in this account."

CASE LAW: BENSON -- NO "PART PERFORMANCE" EXCEPTION; WITHOUT A WRITING ABOUT THE PROPERTY THERE IS NO TRANSMUTATION
In In re Marriage of Benson (2005), a husband testified that he had deeded his community interest in the family home to his wife's trust in exchange for her oral promise to sign a writing making his retirement accounts his separate property; no such writing was ever made. The lower courts treated the husband's performance of his side of the bargain as an adequate substitute for the wife's express written declaration. The California Supreme Court reversed. It held that section 852(a) does not operate like the general statute of frauds, in which the requirement of a basic writing is subject to an implied exception for part performance; that the court found no evidence the Legislature intended to incorporate traditional exceptions to the statute of frauds into section 852; and that, given MacDonald's insistence on a special writing expressly changing the character of the disputed property, section 852(a) cannot be satisfied where there is no writing about the subject property at all and a transmutation would have to be inferred from acts surrounding the disputed agreement. The court summarized the statute as blocking efforts to transmute marital property based on evidence -- oral, behavioral, or documentary -- that is easily manipulated and unreliable.

CASE LAW: DECISIONS BENSON DESCRIBES -- CHANGES OF REGISTRATION, POSSESSION, OR RELIANCE ON AN ORAL PROMISE ARE NOT EXPRESS DECLARATIONS
Benson observed that decisions after MacDonald had adhered closely to it and declined to find a valid transmutation absent express written language to that effect. As Benson described them: in Estate of Bibb (2001), a Department of Motor Vehicles printout changed a vehicle's registration, not its ownership; in In re Marriage of Barneson (1999), written brokerage instructions changed possession, not ownership, of stock; and in In re Marriage of Campbell (1999), a wife acquired no interest in her husband's home where she spent her own money remodeling it after he promised to share title, because section 852(a) is not satisfied solely by one spouse's detrimental reliance on the other's oral promise to transmute. Benson added that a contrary view would threaten to resurrect the easy-transmutation rule the Legislature repudiated when it enacted section 852.

CASE LAW: BENSON -- THE SPOUSAL FIDUCIARY DUTY DOES NOT SUPPLY A TRANSMUTATION THAT SECTION 852 DENIES
The husband in Benson also argued that strict enforcement of section 852(a) was unnecessary because spouses owe each other a fiduciary duty of the highest good faith and fair dealing under Family Code section 721(b), and that denying the transmutation gave his wife an unfair advantage. The Supreme Court rejected the argument. It noted that the presumption of undue influence under section 721(b) operates to undo a transmutation that is so one-sided as to be the product of undue influence, whereas the husband was invoking the fiduciary relationship to establish a transmutation that did not comply with section 852(a); and it held that, absent a transmutation that otherwise satisfies section 852(a), there is no basis for applying the presumption of undue influence under section 721(b). The court added that the two statutes protect marital transactions from the same adverse influences: an express written agreement prevents spouses from inadvertently transmuting property through oral, implied, or other easy means, and also deters false transmutation claims after the marriage ends.

CASE LAW: VALLI -- PROPERTY BOUGHT FROM A THIRD PARTY WITH COMMUNITY FUNDS IN ONE SPOUSE'S NAME IS COMMUNITY PROPERTY ABSENT AN EXPRESS DECLARATION
In In re Marriage of Valli (2014), a husband used community funds during a 20-year marriage to buy a $3.75 million policy on his life, naming his wife as the policy's sole owner and beneficiary. The Court of Appeal had held the policy was the wife's separate property, reasoning that the transmutation statutes apply only to interspousal transactions and not to a spouse's acquisition of property from a third party. The California Supreme Court unanimously reversed and held that, unless the statutory transmutation requirements have been met, the policy is community property. Restating MacDonald, the court said that to satisfy the express-declaration requirement, a writing signed by the adversely affected spouse must expressly state that the character or ownership of the property at issue is being changed. It rejected the purported exemption for purchases from third parties, reasoning that the distinction bore no relation to the Legislature's concerns and would produce arbitrary results, and that the statute's own exception for inexpensive personal gifts -- most of which are bought from third parties -- implies that other purchases are subject to the requirement. In a footnote, the court stated that enactment of the transmutation statutes abrogated earlier judicial decisions inconsistent with them, and that the portion of In re Marriage of Lucas (1980) that had inferred a gift of community funds from a husband's failure to object when title to a motor home was taken in the wife's name alone is no longer good law.

expectedJSON.body: In Estate of MacDonald (1990), the California Supreme Court construed the express-declaration requirement, then codified at Civil Code section 5110.730, subdivision (a), and now found in Family Code section 852, subdivision (a). The court traced the statute to a 1984 recommendation of the California Law Revision Commission. As the court recounted, the Commission had observed that under prior California law it was quite easy for spouses to transmute both real and personal property, because a transmutation could be found based on oral statements or implications from the conduct of the spouses, and that this rule of easy transmutation had generated extensive litigation in dissolution proceedings and encouraged a spouse, after the marriage ended, to transform a passing comment into an agreement or even to commit perjury by manufacturing an oral or implied transmutation. The court concluded that the statute was intended to remedy problems that arose when courts found transmutations on the basis of evidence the Legislature considered unreliable, and that the Legislature intended not only to invalidate purely oral transmutations but also to invalidate some claimed transmutations even though some form of writing existed.

expectedJSON.body: The husband in Benson also argued that strict enforcement of section 852(a) was unnecessary because spouses owe each other a fiduciary duty of the highest good faith and fair dealing under Family Code section 721(b), and that denying the transmutation gave his wife an unfair advantage. The Supreme Court rejected the argument. It noted that the presumption of undue influence under section 721(b) operates to undo a transmutation that is so one-sided as to be the product of undue influence, whereas the husband was invoking the fiduciary relationship to establish a transmutation that did not comply with section 852(a); and it held that, absent a transmutation that otherwise satisfies section 852(a), there is no basis for applying the presumption of undue influence under section 721(b). The court added that the two statutes protect marital transactions from the same adverse influences: an express written agreement prevents spouses from inadvertently transmuting property through oral, implied, or other easy means, and also deters false transmutation claims after the marriage ends.

expectedJSON.body: In In re Marriage of Valli (2014), a husband used community funds during a 20-year marriage to buy a $3.75 million policy on his life, naming his wife as the policy's sole owner and beneficiary. The Court of Appeal had held the policy was the wife's separate property, reasoning that the transmutation statutes apply only to interspousal transactions and not to a spouse's acquisition of property from a third party. The California Supreme Court unanimously reversed and held that, unless the statutory transmutation requirements have been met, the policy is community property. Restating MacDonald, the court said that to satisfy the express-declaration requirement, a writing signed by the adversely affected spouse must expressly state that the character or ownership of the property at issue is being changed. It rejected the purported exemption for purchases from third parties, reasoning that the distinction bore no relation to the Legislature's concerns and would produce arbitrary results, and that the statute's own exception for inexpensive personal gifts -- most of which are bought from third parties -- implies that other purchases are subject to the requirement. In a footnote, the court stated that enactment of the transmutation statutes abrogated earlier judicial decisions inconsistent with them, and that the portion of In re Marriage of Lucas (1980) that had inferred a gift of community funds from a husband's failure to object when title to a motor home was taken in the wife's name alone is no longer good law.

The Supreme Court held this reasoning erroneous. Without deciding whether the section 662 presumption ever applies in marital dissolution proceedings, the court held that, assuming it may sometimes apply, it does not apply when it conflicts with the transmutation statutes. Because the husband never expressly declared in writing that he gave up his community interest in the policy bought with community funds, the court agreed with the trial court's characterization of the policy as community property.

expectedJSON.body: In In re Brace (2020), answering a question certified by the Ninth Circuit in a bankruptcy case, the California Supreme Court extended Valli beyond marital dissolution. It held that Evidence Code section 662's form-of-title presumption does not apply when it conflicts with the Family Code section 760 community property presumption, and that when a married couple uses community funds to acquire property with joint tenancy title on or after January 1, 1975, the property is presumptively community property in a dispute between the couple and a bankruptcy trustee. The court declined to confine Valli to dissolution proceedings, finding no basis in the text, purpose, or history of section 760 to do so. It then answered whether a joint tenancy deed alone can satisfy section 852: for property acquired on or after January 1, 1985, joint tenancy titling of property acquired with community funds is not sufficient by itself to transmute community property into separate property. For joint tenancy property acquired between January 1, 1975 and December 31, 1984, the act of taking title as joint tenants is likewise insufficient in itself to prove a transmutation, although a court may consider the manner of taking title in deciding whether the spouses had an oral agreement or common understanding; and joint tenancy property acquired with community funds before January 1, 1975 is presumptively separate property.

expectedJSON.body: Section 852 contains three limits on its own reach. First, under subdivision (c), the writing and express-declaration requirement does not apply to a gift between the spouses of clothing, wearing apparel, jewelry, or other tangible articles of a personal nature that is used solely or principally by the recipient spouse and that is not substantial in value taking into account the circumstances of the marriage; Valli read this exception as implying that gifts outside it -- because they are substantial in value or are not personal articles -- are transmutations subject to the requirement. Second, under subdivision (d), nothing in the section affects the law governing characterization of property in which separate and community property are commingled or otherwise combined. Third, under subdivision (e), the section does not apply to or affect a transmutation made before January 1, 1985, and the law that would otherwise be applicable continues to govern such a transmutation; as Brace explained, for transmutations before 1985 a written agreement is not required, and a valid transmutation can be shown by substantial evidence of an oral or written agreement or a common understanding between the spouses.
